# UMAP in manifoldsR

`manifoldsR` provides a very rapid implementation of
[UMAP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03426), based on the brilliant work in the
[uwot](https://github.com/jlmelville/uwot) package. Everything runs in Rust,
R is purely the interface, and the aim is to push the algorithm even further
on speed.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(manifoldsR)
library(magrittr)
library(ggplot2)
library(data.table)
```

## Intro

UMAP works by constructing a weighted k-nearest neighbour graph in the
high-dimensional space (see the knn_searches vignette for more details here!),
where edge weights reflect the likelihood that two points are connected given
their distance under a local, adaptive metric. It then minimises a
cross-entropy loss between this high-dimensional graph and a low-dimensional
analogue, pulling connected nodes together and pushing unconnected ones apart.
This objective is why **UMAP excels at preserving cluster structure**: if two
points are unlikely neighbours in high dimensions, the repulsion term drives
them apart in the embedding, producing clean separation.
The flip side is that UMAP has
**no incentive to preserve the relative distances along a continuum**. For
trajectory or manifold data where the meaningful signal is a smooth
progression, the loss treats weakly-connected distant points as things to repel
rather than as part of a coherent structure. Continuous manifolds tend to get
torn apart into spurious clusters. Distances and even topology within an
embedding should **therefore be interpreted with caution**.
[UMAP is a visualisation tool, not a metric space!](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011288)

## Running UMAP

The default optimiser is a parallel version of Adam, the same idea `uwot`
uses in `umap2()`. The gradients for each node are collected in parallel and
then applied in one go, so it scales with your cores, and the same seed gives
you the same embedding every time. There is also a sequential Adam
(`optimiser = "adam"`), but the parallel one is the one you want.

We are going to generate three different data sets to showcase the strengths
(and weaknesses) of UMAP:

```{r}
#| label: synthetic data
cluster_data <- manifold_synthetic_data(
  type = "cluster",
  n_samples = 25000L
)

swissroll_data <- manifold_synthetic_data(
  type = "swiss_roll",
  n_samples = 1000L
)

trajectory_data <- manifold_synthetic_data(
  type = "trajectory",
  n_samples = 25000L
)
```

### Clustered data

Let's start with something UMAP does well: visualise well separated clusters.
We will first contrast this against standard PCA to have a baseline...

```{r}
#| label: clustered data - pca
pca_clusters <- prcomp(cluster_data$data)

pca_clusters_df <- as.data.table(pca_clusters$x[, 1:2]) %>%
  `colnames<-`(c("PC1", "PC2")) %>%
  .[, cluster := as.factor(cluster_data$membership)]

ggplot(
  data = pca_clusters_df,
  mapping = aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)
) +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(colour = cluster), size = 0.75, alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("PCA on clustered data")
```

PCA does an okay job here, but several of the clusters are clearly mixed.
The separation likely sits in other combinations of the PCs. Let's see what
UMAP can do in just two dimensions.

```{r}
#| label: clustered data - umap
umap_clusters <- umap(
  data = cluster_data$data,
  k = 15L
)

umap_clustered_df <- as.data.table(umap_clusters) %>%
  `colnames<-`(c("UMAP1", "UMAP2")) %>%
  .[, cluster := as.factor(cluster_data$membership)]

ggplot(
  data = umap_clustered_df,
  mapping = aes(x = UMAP1, y = UMAP2)
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(colour = cluster),
    alpha = 0.5,
    size = 0.75
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("UMAP on clustered data")
```

UMAP cleanly separates the individual clusters (as expected). In other cases,
UMAP does worse... Let's look at the Swiss roll.

### Swiss roll

```{r}
#| label: swissroll data - pca
pca_swiss_roll <- prcomp(swissroll_data$data)

pca_swiss_roll_df <- as.data.table(pca_swiss_roll$x[, 1:2]) %>%
  `colnames<-`(c("PC1", "PC2")) %>%
  .[, z_axis := swissroll_data$data[, 3]]

ggplot(
  data = pca_swiss_roll_df,
  mapping = aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(fill = z_axis),
    shape = 21,
    size = 2,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("PCA on swissroll")
```

PCA clearly captures the Swiss roll structure. How does UMAP perform here ... ?

```{r}
#| label: swissroll data - umap
umap_swissroll <- umap(
  data = swissroll_data$data,
  knn_method = "exhaustive",
  k = 10L # reduced because smaller
)

umap_swissroll_df <- as.data.table(umap_swissroll) %>%
  `colnames<-`(c("UMAP1", "UMAP2")) %>%
  .[, z_axis := swissroll_data$data[, 3]]

ggplot(
  data = umap_swissroll_df,
  mapping = aes(x = UMAP1, y = UMAP2)
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(fill = z_axis),
    shape = 21,
    size = 2,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("UMAP on swissroll")
```

UMAP rips apart the Swiss roll. Due to the nature of the loss, it is not a
great algorithm for data with a continuum-type manifold. The trajectory data
shows the same problem.

### Trajectory

PCA first again.

```{r}
#| label: trajectory data - pca
pca_trajectory <- prcomp(trajectory_data$data)

pca_trajectory_df <- as.data.table(pca_trajectory$x[, 1:2]) %>%
  `colnames<-`(c("PC1", "PC2")) %>%
  .[, branch := trajectory_data$membership]

# will mix the labels to visualise the continuum better
ggplot(
  data = pca_trajectory_df[
    sample(1:nrow(pca_trajectory_df), nrow(pca_trajectory_df)),
  ],
  mapping = aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(colour = branch),
    alpha = 0.5,
    size = 0.75
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "turbo") +
  ggtitle("PCA on trajectory data")
```

We can appreciate the branching and the continuum in the data.

```{r}
#| label: trajectory data - umap
umap_trajectory <- umap(
  data = trajectory_data$data,
  knn_method = "exhaustive"
)

umap_trajectory_df <- as.data.table(umap_trajectory) %>%
  `colnames<-`(c("UMAP1", "UMAP2")) %>%
  .[, branch := trajectory_data$membership]

ggplot(
  data = umap_trajectory_df[
    sample(1:nrow(umap_trajectory_df), nrow(umap_trajectory_df)),
  ],
  mapping = aes(x = UMAP1, y = UMAP2)
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(colour = branch),
    alpha = 0.5,
    size = 0.75
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "turbo") +
  ggtitle("UMAP on trajectory data")
```

Here we see the clear problem of UMAP. Instead of the continuum in the
manifold, we end up with distinct clusters and some bleeding in between them.
That does not represent the underlying data at all.

## Using pre-computed kNN parameters

Want to test a range of parameters while keeping the number of neighbours
constant? Compute the kNN graph once and hand the `NearestNeighbours` object
to `umap()`:

```{r}
#| label: umap - use pre-computed kNN
precomputed_knn <- generate_knn_graph(
  data = cluster_data$data,
  k = 15L,
  .verbose = FALSE
)

umap_clusters_from_knn <- umap(
  data = cluster_data$data,
  knn = precomputed_knn,
  k = 15L
)

umap_clustered_from_knn_df <- as.data.table(umap_clusters_from_knn) %>%
  `colnames<-`(c("UMAP1", "UMAP2")) %>%
  .[, cluster := as.factor(cluster_data$membership)]

ggplot(
  data = umap_clustered_from_knn_df,
  mapping = aes(x = UMAP1, y = UMAP2)
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(colour = cluster),
    alpha = 0.5,
    size = 0.75
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("UMAP on pre-computed kNN")
```

And a quick re-run with a different `min_dist`:

```{r}
#| label: umap - different parameters
umap_clusters_from_knn <- umap(
  data = cluster_data$data,
  knn = precomputed_knn,
  min_dist = 1.0, # let's make the min_dist bigger
  k = 15L
)

umap_clustered_from_knn_df <- as.data.table(umap_clusters_from_knn) %>%
  `colnames<-`(c("UMAP1", "UMAP2")) %>%
  .[, cluster := as.factor(cluster_data$membership)]

ggplot(
  data = umap_clustered_from_knn_df,
  mapping = aes(x = UMAP1, y = UMAP2)
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(colour = cluster),
    alpha = 0.5,
    size = 0.75
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("UMAP on pre-computed kNN (min_dist = 1.0)")
```

## umap-learn behaviour: SGD

The original UMAP (and `umap-learn`, and `uwot::umap()`) optimises with plain
stochastic gradient descent. If you want embeddings that look like those, pick
one of the two SGD optimisers:

- `"sgd"`: single-threaded, reproducible with a given seed.
- `"sgd_parallel"`: lock-free, [Hogwild!](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.5730)
  style. All threads write to the shared embedding without locks, which is
  where the speed comes from. The price: with more than one thread it is
  **not reproducible** run to run, even with the same seed.

Like `umap-learn`, both drop to 200 epochs above 10k samples unless you set
`n_epochs` yourself.

```{r}
#| label: umap - sgd
umap_clusters_sgd <- umap(
  data = cluster_data$data,
  knn = precomputed_knn,
  umap_params = params_umap(optimiser = "sgd"),
  k = 15L,
  .verbose = FALSE
)

umap_clusters_sgd_par <- umap(
  data = cluster_data$data,
  knn = precomputed_knn,
  umap_params = params_umap(optimiser = "sgd_parallel"),
  k = 15L,
  .verbose = FALSE
)

umap_sgd_df <- rbind(
  as.data.table(umap_clusters_sgd)[, optimiser := "sgd"],
  as.data.table(umap_clusters_sgd_par)[, optimiser := "sgd_parallel"]
) %>%
  `colnames<-`(c("UMAP1", "UMAP2", "optimiser")) %>%
  .[, cluster := as.factor(rep(cluster_data$membership, 2L))]

ggplot(
  data = umap_sgd_df,
  mapping = aes(x = UMAP1, y = UMAP2)
) +
  geom_point(
    mapping = aes(colour = cluster),
    alpha = 0.5,
    size = 0.75
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~optimiser, scales = "free") +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("UMAP with the SGD optimisers")
```

Same picture, one of them just gets there using all your cores. On
reproducibility, don't take my word for it:

```{r}
#| label: umap - reproducibility
run_twice <- function(optimiser) {
  purrr::map(1:2, \(i) {
    umap(
      data = cluster_data$data,
      knn = precomputed_knn,
      umap_params = params_umap(optimiser = optimiser),
      seed = 42L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  })
}

adam_par_runs <- run_twice("adam_parallel")
sgd_par_runs <- run_twice("sgd_parallel")

c(
  adam_parallel = identical(adam_par_runs[[1]], adam_par_runs[[2]]),
  sgd_parallel = identical(sgd_par_runs[[1]], sgd_par_runs[[2]])
)
```

## Benchmarks

How does this compare against other UMAP implementations? Let's do a
benchmark:

```{r}
#| label: python env
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("microbenchmark", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("reticulate", quietly = TRUE)
# set up the venv for the Python part/dependencies
local({
  env_name <- "r-manifolds"
  py_pkgs <- c("phate", "umap-learn", "numpy", "scipy")

  if (!reticulate::virtualenv_exists(env_name)) {
    reticulate::virtualenv_create(env_name)
    reticulate::virtualenv_install(env_name, packages = py_pkgs)
  }

  if (!reticulate::py_available()) {
    reticulate::use_virtualenv(env_name, required = TRUE)
  }

  missing_pkgs <- Filter(
    Negate(reticulate::py_module_available),
    c("phate", "umap")
  )
  if (length(missing_pkgs) > 0L) {
    reticulate::virtualenv_install(env_name, packages = py_pkgs)
  }
})
```

```{r}
#| label: umap - benchmark small
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("microbenchmark", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("reticulate", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("umap", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("uwot", quietly = TRUE)
benchmark_data <- manifold_synthetic_data(
  type = "cluster",
  n_samples = 5000L
)

umap_py <- reticulate::import("umap")

# initialise numba properly via JIT for fair comparison
# run a small dataset...
test_reducer <- umap_py$UMAP(
  n_neighbors = 15L,
  n_jobs = parallel::detectCores() - 1L
)
test <- test_reducer$fit_transform(benchmark_data$data[1:500, ])

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  # umap version in pure R
  umap = {
    umap::umap(
      d = benchmark_data$data,
      method = "naive"
    )
  },
  umap_reticulate = {
    reducer <- umap_py$UMAP(
      n_neighbors = 15L,
      n_jobs = parallel::detectCores() - 1L
    )
    reducer$fit_transform(benchmark_data$data)
  },
  # uwot - umap, for example used in Seurat
  uwot = {
    uwot::umap(X = benchmark_data$data)
  },
  # uwot - umap2 version with parallel Adam under the hood
  # the approach that was also taken by manifoldsR
  uwot_v2 = {
    uwot::umap2(X = benchmark_data$data)
  },
  # the manifolds version
  manifold_umap = {
    umap(
      data = benchmark_data$data,
      k = 15L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  times = 1L # single comparison for speed
)
```

The standard R version is slow (as expected). The Python version (with numba
behind the scenes) via reticulate gives some speed-up, once the numba parts
are JIT compiled. `uwot::umap2()` and `manifoldsR` are the fastest here.
Let's pit them against each other on a larger data set, Adam against Adam and
SGD against SGD. `uwot::umap()` gets all cores for the SGD step, which makes
it lock-free and non-reproducible too, so the comparison is fair.

```{r}
#| label: umap - benchmark large
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("microbenchmark", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("uwot", quietly = TRUE)
benchmark_data_2 <- manifold_synthetic_data(
  type = "cluster",
  n_samples = 50000L
)

n_cores <- parallel::detectCores()

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  # parallel Adam
  uwot_v2 = {
    uwot::umap2(X = benchmark_data_2$data)
  },
  manifold_adam_parallel = {
    umap(
      data = benchmark_data_2$data,
      k = 15L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  # multi-threaded SGD
  uwot_sgd = {
    uwot::umap(
      X = benchmark_data_2$data,
      n_threads = n_cores,
      n_sgd_threads = n_cores
    )
  },
  manifold_sgd_parallel = {
    umap(
      data = benchmark_data_2$data,
      k = 15L,
      umap_params = params_umap(optimiser = "sgd_parallel"),
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  times = 1L # single comparison for speed
)
```

Optimised memory layouts, aggressive in-lining, heavy parallelism and look-up
tables (LUTs) make this version **fast**: likely(?) the fastest UMAP available
in R. Memory stays minimal too, as the data lives in Rust from the moment it
enters the kernel until the embedding is fitted. No round tripping through R,
just compiled code throughout. The different nearest neighbour search
algorithms give additional flexibility.
